levels.name: Ben, 24, Barista
levels.story: The 8 levels of dating app burnout. Level 1. Null Matches, aber 40 Euro im Monat für Fake-Profile – warum zahle ich eigentlich dafür, dass mir ein Drachenfrucht-Millionär ins Gesicht lacht? I have swiped right six hundred times this week on local dating apps in Brooklyn, but my screen stays stubbornly dark. My phone buzzes with a notification. It is just an ad for a premium subscription costing $39.99 a month. The tired potato waitress drops my lukewarm black coffee on the sticky laminate table without looking at me. A sleek dragon fruit man strolls past my booth in a designer trench coat, glancing at my glowing forehead with sheer pity. You are wasting thumb energy on ghosts, kid. Swipe left on your entire pathetic life. My heart drops into my soggy fries. Then my phone screen suddenly lights up with an incoming video call from an unknown number. Das siehst du in Level 2. You'll see that in Level 2.

levels.name: Maya, 26, Graphic Designer
levels.story: The 8 levels of dating app burnout. Level 2. Drei Wochen Situationship und dann eine Absage per Text drei Minuten vor dem Date – während die Möwe neben mir hämisch lacht. I am sitting in a cramped Astoria apartment paying $1,850 a month, staring at three dots on my screen that have been pulsing for forty minutes. My match, a smooth orange guy named Leo, promised we would get $8 artisanal matcha lattes together at noon. Instead, my phone lights up with a cold cancellation text. Something came up at the office, rain check? A smug carrot woman leans against my doorway, sipping organic juice and scoffing at my phone. Du wirst niemals mehr als eine Notlösung für den Dienstagabend sein. Nobody buys groceries when they are just window shopping. My studio apartment feels instantly smaller. Then my intercom buzzes loudly downstairs. Das siehst du in Level 3. You'll see that in Level 3.

levels.name: Leo, 29, Financial Analyst
levels.story: The 8 levels of dating app burnout. Level 3. Fünfundvierzig Matches, aber ich sitze allein im Penthouse und ghoste drei Frauen, bis mein eigener Spiegel mich anspuckt. I make $95,000 a year working eighty hours in Manhattan, yet my thumb keeps mindlessly swiping through endless profiles like I am shopping on Amazon. My smart TV plays background noise while my phone buzzes incessantly with unread messages. A sharp broccoli man in a crisp tailored suit walks into my open-concept kitchen, tossing my apartment keys onto the marble island. You are treating human beings like disposable fast food, man. A full cart means nothing if you refuse to check out. The silence in my expensive apartment feels deafening, and as I look at my glowing screen, I suddenly slap myself in the face in pure frustration, realizing I am completely addicted. Then my front door security camera chimes with an unexpected visitor. Das siehst du in Level 4. You'll see that in Level 4.

levels.name: Sam, 25, Musician
levels.story: The 8 levels of dating app burnout. Level 4. Neunundachtzig Matches und niemand hört meine Musik, weil alle nur den Gratis-Eintritt abgreifen wollen. I make $42,000 a year teaching guitar lessons and gigging on weekends. A lovely lemon woman named Clara sits on the barstool beside me, nursing a ginger ale and listening to my set. My phone notifications keep pinging with matches from people who only want free concert tickets. A bitter strawberry girl with bright red seeds and dark sunglasses leans over the sticky wooden bar top. Niemand hört zu, sie wollen nur den Gratis-Eintritt. Nobody buys the instrument when they just came for the concert. My guitar strings suddenly feel loose and out of tune. Then my phone rings with an urgent call from my landlord. Das siehst du in Level 5. You'll see that in Level 5.

levels.name: The Alchemist, ???, Unknown
levels.story: The 8 levels of dating app burnout. Level 8. Alle Apps gelöscht, Hände zitern beim Entzug – wieso fühlt sich echte Freiheit im Park plötzlich wie illegaler Entzug an? I am sitting on a wooden park bench in Washington Square Park watching real people actually talk to each other without looking at glowing screens. All the characters from every level walk past my bench together, smiling and laughing under the afternoon sun. A wise old pineapple vendor hands me a fresh glass of lemonade without asking for my stats or my salary. The digital numbers on everyone's foreheads suddenly flicker, fade out, and disappear completely into the warm air. We traded algorithms for reality, and nobody checked a screen once. The entire city feels alive for the first time in years. Which toxic modern trap should we expose next in our city?
